content: In South Asia, where home deliveries and neonatal mortality rates are high, three studies evaluated the application of chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord compared to standard dry cord care. These studies demonstrated significant reductions in neonatal mortality and omphalitis. The number of postnatal contacts in these studies ranged from one to seven, with two studies focusing on visits during the first week of life only. The World Health Organization (WHO) has made recommendations on postnatal care for mothers and newborns based on evidence reviews. No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have directly compared the effects of varying numbers and timings of postnatal contacts. Approximately 40% of neonatal deaths occur within the first 24 hours of life, accounting for nearly three-quarters of asphyxia-related deaths and over 40% of prematurity-related deaths. Additionally, about 40% of prematurity-related and sepsis-related deaths, as well as one-quarter of asphyxia-related deaths, occur between days 1 and 7 of life. Around 30% of sepsis-related deaths occur in the second week of life, with one-quarter occurring in the last two weeks of the neonatal period. Studies that showed benefits of breastfeeding promotion interventions included at least one contact during the first week of life, with many also including visits in the second week. The number of contacts in these studies ranged from one to seven. Two of the three studies demonstrating the benefits of chlorhexidine application to the umbilical cord involved seven contacts within the first 14 days of life. WHO strongly recommends home visits during the first week after birth for the care of mothers and newborns. These visits are often linked to home visits during pregnancy, which promote antenatal care utilization but do not replace it. Depending on the health system, these visits can be conducted by midwives, skilled providers, or well-trained and supervised community health workers (CHWs). Postnatal contacts may also occur during clinic visits. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), home visits by CHWs have been shown to reduce neonatal and perinatal mortality. A systematic review identified five cluster-randomized controlled trials (CRCTs) from South Asia (Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan) involving over 100,000 participants. These trials included at least two home visits by female CHWs during the first week after birth (on days 1 and 3). CHWs promoted optimal newborn care practices, such as early initiation of exclusive breastfeeding (EBF), keeping the baby warm, hygienic care, and seeking care for illness. Community mobilization activities were also implemented to improve intervention uptake. In four of the trials, CHWs were trained to identify sick newborns by assessing danger signs during home visits and referring them to health facilities. In one trial in Bangladesh, CHWs were trained to administer intramuscular antibiotics when referral was not possible. The impact of CHW home visits on neonatal mortality was evaluated in all five CRCTs, with evidence graded as high quality. The effect size was greater in settings with very high baseline neonatal mortality rates (NMR > 50 per 1,000 live births). Evidence from three CRCTs also demonstrated a significant reduction in perinatal mortality, with high-quality evidence. However, all studies were conducted in South Asia, and results from two African studies are pending. No data are available on potential harms related to home visits. Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) is strongly recommended for all babies from birth until six months of age. Mothers should be counseled and supported for EBF during every postnatal contact. Moderate-quality evidence indicates that exclusively breastfed neonates have a lower risk of all-cause mortality and infection-related mortality in the first month of life compared to partially breastfed neonates. Low-quality evidence suggests that EBF reduces the risk of sepsis, acute respiratory infections (ARI), and diarrhea morbidity in the first month of life. However, evidence is insufficient to compare the benefits of exclusive versus predominant breastfeeding on neonatal mortality and morbidity. The application of 4% chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump during the first week of life is recommended for newborns born at home in settings with high neonatal mortality (≥30 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births). Clean, dry cord care is recommended for newborns born in health facilities or at home in low neonatal mortality settings. Chlorhexidine use in these situations may be considered only to replace harmful traditional substances, such as cow dung, applied to the cord stump. In conclusion, evidence from South Asia suggests that home visits by CHWs during the first week of life, combined with other interventions, are effective in reducing neonatal and perinatal mortality. Exclusive breastfeeding and chlorhexidine application to the umbilical cord are also critical interventions for improving neonatal outcomes.
